cs-01.title: What a Computer Does
explain: A computer is a machine that takes **input**, performs **processing** on it according to fixed rules, and produces **output**. When needed, it can **store** results and use them again later. Receiving letters from a keyboard (input), counting the number of letters (processing), and showing a number on the screen (output) all fit into this framework.

All information inside a computer is ultimately represented as **bits**. A bit is the smallest unit, holding either 0 or 1. Text, pictures, and sound are also handled by converting them into agreed-upon groups of 0s and 1s.

When several bits are combined, more distinct things can be told apart. One bit can distinguish 2 values, two bits can distinguish 2 × 2 = 4 values, and three bits can distinguish 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 values. Each time one more bit is added, the number of possible values doubles.

A number notation that uses only 0 and 1 is the **binary** system. In the **decimal** system we normally use, each place is worth a power of ten such as 1, 10, or 100. In binary, the place values from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on. Adding the place values of all positions that contain a 1 gives the decimal number.

cs-02.title: Algorithms and Flowcharts
explain: An **algorithm** is a sequence of steps for solving a problem. A person can follow it like a recipe, or a computer can follow it.

For an algorithm to be good, it must satisfy several conditions.
- Its **input and output** are clear. It is fixed what it receives and what it produces.
- It is **unambiguous**. Each step is read with the same meaning by anyone who carries it out.
- It is **finite**. It always ends at some point.
- Each step can actually be **carried out**.

A **flowchart** is a drawing of an algorithm. Its symbols are fixed.
- Oval: start and end
- Rectangle: a process (one task)
- Diamond: a condition check. The path splits depending on yes or no
- Arrow: the direction of flow
A flowchart is read by following the arrows one step at a time. All code and flowchart problems in this department are solved by tracing by hand, so there is no need to run a program.

cs-03.title: Sense of Data Structures
explain: A **data structure** is a way of deciding how to arrange multiple pieces of data. The same data can be easier or harder to insert and retrieve depending on how it is stored.

A **list** is data arranged in a single line in order. Each item is referred to by its position, as in 'the nth item'. In this department, the first item is counted as position 1. (Many programming languages count from 0, but here the counting is unified to start from 1.)

A **stack** is a structure in which items are inserted and removed from only one end. The item inserted last comes out first. It is like picking up plates from the top of a pile. Insertion is called a push, and removal is called a pop.
A **queue** is a structure in which items are inserted at one end and removed from the other end. The item inserted first comes out first. It is like waiting your turn in a line.

A **tree** is a structure that branches from top to bottom. The node at the very top is the **root**, and each box is a **node**. A node above is the **parent**, and a node connected by a line below it is a **child**. A node with no children is called a **leaf**. A folder containing folders on a computer is a good example of a tree.

cs-04.title: Variables, Conditions, and Loops
explain: When writing an algorithm in text, **pseudocode** is used rather than any specific programming language. It is loosely code-like text meant for people to read, with no strict rules. All the code in this lesson is traced by hand, and nothing is run anywhere.

A **variable** is a named value box. Putting a value into it is called **assignment** and is written `x ← 5`. It means 'put 5 into the box named x'. A box holds only one value at a time, so when a new value is put in, the old value disappears.
As in `y ← x + 1`, the right side is calculated first, and the result is put into the box on the left. `x ← x + 1` means 'add 1 to the current value of x and put the result back into x'.

A **condition** is a judgment that splits the path.
- `If x > 3 then`: the line below is performed only when this is true.
- `Else`: the line below is performed when the condition is false.

A **loop** repeats the same task several times. `Repeat for i from 1 to 4` changes i to 1, 2, 3, and 4 and performs the inner line four times. There are also forms that repeat while a condition is true, such as `Repeat while x < 10`. In this case, if the value inside is not changed so that the condition eventually becomes false, the loop never ends.
Value tracing is a method of following the lines one at a time and writing down the values of the variables in a table. It is the most reliable way to read code.

When i is 1, sum becomes 0 + 1 = 1. When i is 2, it becomes 1 + 2 = 3. When i is 3, it becomes 3 + 3 = 6. When the loop ends, sum is 6.

cs-05.title: Sense of Efficiency
explain: When several algorithms solve the same problem, we can compare which one is more **efficient**. Here, the amount of work is counted as the 'number of comparisons'. One comparison means checking one value in the list against the value being sought.

**Linear search** checks the list one item at a time, starting from the beginning. In the **worst case**, the value being sought is at the very end or not present at all, so the number of comparisons equals the number of items. If there are 200 items, the maximum is 200 comparisons.

**Binary search** can be used when the list is **sorted in ascending order**. Compare with the middle value: if it is equal, stop; if the sought value is larger, keep only the right half; if it is smaller, keep only the left half. Repeat the same process on the remaining half. Each comparison reduces the candidates to half or less.

When there are 7 or 15 items, which are one less than a power of 2 (2 multiplied by itself a number of times), the candidates shrink neatly: 7 → 3 → 1, and 15 → 7 → 3 → 1. With 7 items, there are at most 3 comparisons, and with 15 items, at most 4. Even when the number of items roughly doubles, the number of comparisons increases by only 1. This is why binary search is fast on large lists.
However, binary search has a cost. The list must be sorted. If you look only at the middle of an unsorted list and discard half, you may throw away the value you are looking for.

cs-06.title: How the Web Works
explain: Opening a web page is a conversation between two computers. The side asking to be shown the page is the **client** (usually a browser), and the side that holds the page and sends it back is the **server**.

The request sent by the client is a **request**, and the answer the server returns is a **response**. This agreed-upon way of conversing is called HTTP. An address that begins with `https` adds a method for protecting the content exchanged over HTTP.

A web address (URL) tells you what you are asking for and where it is. Breaking down `https://example.com/photos/cat.html` gives the following.
- `https`: the conversation method
- `example.com`: the name of the server
- `/photos/cat.html`: the path that points to which data is inside that server

The server name is converted into a numeric address used for communication between computers, and then the request is sent there. The response carries a number called a **status code**. 200 means the request was processed successfully, and 404 means the requested data could not be found.

A successful response contains the page content as text. This text is written in a format called HTML, and the browser reads it and draws the title, paragraphs, and picture placeholders on the screen. The server does not draw the screen and send it; it sends the content, and the browser does the drawing.

cs-07.title: Asymptotic Complexity and Sorting Algorithms
explain: In the earlier lesson "Sense of Efficiency," we got a feel for efficiency. This time we turn that feel into precise language. Two programs that solve the same problem may be about equally fast with 100 data items, but with 1 million items one may take 1 second while the other takes several hours. **Asymptotic complexity** describes the **shape** in which the running time grows as the input becomes large.

**Big-O notation** $O(f(n))$ means that when the input size $n$ is sufficiently large, the running time does not exceed a constant multiple of $f(n)$. Constants and lower-order terms are ignored. $3n^2 + 100n + 7$ is $O(n^2)$. Common growth orders are: $O(1) < O(\log n) < O(n) < O(n\log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n)$. When $n = 10^6$, $n\log_2 n \approx 2 \times 10^7$, but $n^2 = 10^{12}$, a difference of 50,000 times.

Let us compare with sorting. **Insertion sort** inserts each element one by one into the correct position in the already sorted front part. Its worst case is $O(n^2)$, but on nearly sorted data it is close to $O(n)$. **Merge sort** uses **divide and conquer**. It splits the array in half, sorts each half, and merges the two sorted halves by comparing from the front. The splitting step happens $\log_2 n$ times, and merging at each level costs $O(n)$, so the total is $O(n\log n)$.

**Quick sort** splits the data into elements smaller and larger than a reference value (the pivot) and sorts them recursively. Its average is $O(n\log n)$, and it is very fast in practice, but if the pivot is repeatedly chosen poorly, the worst case is $O(n^2)$. It has been proven that any algorithm that sorts using only comparisons has a **lower bound**: in the worst case it cannot make fewer than $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparisons. This is because distinguishing the $n!$ possible orderings requires at least $\log_2 n!$ yes-or-no questions, and this value is roughly $n\log_2 n$.

Limitations: Big-O only describes the **shape of growth** for large $n$. For small inputs, an $O(n\log n)$ algorithm with large constants can be slower than a simple $O(n^2)$ algorithm, so real libraries use a hybrid approach that switches to insertion sort on small segments. Also, memory access patterns (cache memory, covered in the Computer Architecture and Operating Systems branch) greatly affect actual speed. Along with time complexity, **space complexity** must also be considered (merge sort needs $O(n)$ extra memory).

cs-08.title: Trees, Heaps, and Hash Tables: Structures for Fast Search
explain: How data is stored determines the speed of operations. To find a value in an unsorted array, you may have to look at up to $O(n)$ items, but with a suitable structure this can be reduced to $O(\log n)$ or, on average, $O(1)$. This lesson covers three key structures.

A **binary search tree** (BST) places smaller values in the left subtree of each node and larger values in the right subtree. Because you start at the root and descend by comparing, searching, inserting, and deleting are proportional to the **height** of the tree. If the tree is well balanced, the height is $\log_2 n$ and the cost is $O(\log n)$, but if values are inserted in sorted order, the tree stretches to one side, the height becomes $n$, and the cost worsens to $O(n)$. That is why trees that balance themselves, such as AVL trees or red-black trees, are used.

A **heap** is a complete binary tree in which each parent is always smaller than or equal to its children (a min-heap). The smallest value is always at the root, so it can be checked in $O(1)$. Insertion and removal of the minimum swap positions up or down by up to the height, so they cost $O(\log n)$. It is cleanly implemented as an array (the children of index $i$ are $2i+1$ and $2i+2$). It is the standard implementation of a **priority queue**, and it is used in the shortest path algorithm of the next lesson and in operating system scheduling.

A **hash table** converts a key into an array slot number using a **hash function** and accesses it directly. It is the fastest structure, at $O(1)$ on average. A **collision**, in which different keys map to the same slot, cannot be avoided (pigeonhole principle). Collisions are handled either by chaining, which attaches a list to the same slot, or by open addressing, which searches for an empty slot. When the ratio of stored elements to slots, the **load factor**, grows large, collisions increase and operations slow down, so once it exceeds a certain level, the array is enlarged and all elements are placed again.

Criteria and limits: hashing is fast but has **no order**. If you need range searches such as 'all keys between 10 and 20' or sorted traversal, a balanced tree is better. If you need to repeatedly extract the minimum, a heap is the right choice. Hashing can degrade to a worst case of $O(n)$ with a poor hash function or with inputs deliberately designed to cause collisions. You must distinguish between the 'average' and the 'worst case' when describing it.

cs-09.title: Shortest Paths, Dynamic Programming, and NP
explain: A map app finds the fastest route among countless intersections and roads in an instant. A road network is a **graph** (vertices and edges), and finding a route is the **shortest path problem**. This lesson covers two representative algorithms and the world of problems (NP) for which no efficient algorithm is known.

explain.alt: A weighted graph with vertices A, B, C, D, and E. Edge weights: A-B 4, A-C 2, C-B 1, B-D 5, C-D 8, C-E 10, D-E 2.

explain: **Dijkstra's algorithm** finds the shortest distances from one starting point to all vertices when all edge weights are non-negative. The idea: among the vertices whose distance is not yet finalized, choose the vertex with the **currently shortest distance** and finalize it; if a path through that vertex is shorter to a neighbor, update the neighbor's distance (**relaxation**). Implementing this selection with a heap takes $O((V + E)\log V)$. If there are negative weights, a distance already finalized may later become shorter, so Dijkstra's algorithm can be wrong. In that case, the Bellman-Ford algorithm is used.

**Dynamic programming** (DP) divides a large problem into overlapping smaller problems, computes the answer to each smaller problem **only once** and stores it, and reuses it. Two conditions are needed: **optimal substructure** (the optimal solution is composed of optimal solutions to subproblems) and **overlapping subproblems**. Computing Fibonacci numbers by plain recursion repeats the same values exponentially many times, but storing them in a table takes $O(n)$. Shortest paths, the knapsack problem, and string edit distance are solved with DP.

Is there a fast algorithm for every problem? **P** is the set of problems that can be solved in polynomial time, and **NP** is the set of problems for which a given answer can be **verified** in polynomial time. **NP-complete** problems (the decision version of the traveling salesman problem, graph coloring, subset sum) are the hardest problems in NP. If even one of them could be solved in polynomial time, every NP problem could be solved in polynomial time. Whether P = NP is still unresolved, and it is regarded as the greatest open problem in computer science.

In practice, when encountering NP-complete problems, one does not give up. If the input is small, one tries all possibilities; or one uses **approximation algorithms** and **heuristics** that quickly find good solutions; or one exploits special structure in the problem. Limitations: the weights must be defined differently depending on the criterion of 'shortest' (time, distance, or fare), and if the weights keep changing, as with real-time traffic, precomputed answers become outdated.

Step 2: B (3) is finalized → D is updated to $3 + 5 = 8$. D (8) is finalized → E is updated to $8 + 2 = 10$. E (10) is finalized. The shortest distance from A to E is 10, along the path A-C-B-D-E.

Step 2: Building a table gives $f(3) = 3$, $f(4) = 5$, $f(5) = 8$, and $f(6) = 13$. Plain recursion without storage recalculates the same values countless times.

cs-10.title: Pipelining and the Cache Memory Hierarchy
explain: A CPU processes billions of instructions per second. However, fetching data from memory takes as long as executing hundreds of CPU instructions. Two key techniques keep a fast CPU from sitting idle while waiting for slow memory: **pipelining** and **caching**.

Processing one instruction goes through the stages instruction fetch (IF) → instruction decode (ID) → execute (EX) → memory access (MEM) → write-back (WB). **Pipelining** works like a laundry: as soon as the first instruction moves on to the decode stage, the second instruction is fetched. The processing time of each instruction stays the same, but since one instruction finishes every clock cycle, **throughput** can increase by up to the number of stages. On a $k$-stage pipeline, processing $n$ instructions ideally takes $k + n - 1$ clock cycles.

**Hazards** that stall the pipeline are: **data hazards**, where the next instruction must use the result of the previous one right away (mitigated by forwarding, which passes the result directly to the next stage); **control hazards**, where the next instruction must be fetched before the outcome of a branch is known (mitigated by branch prediction); and **structural hazards**, where two instructions try to use the same resource at the same time. Because of hazards, the actual speedup is smaller than the ideal.

explain.alt: A memory hierarchy pyramid. From top to bottom: registers (under 1 ns), cache (about 1 to 10 ns), main memory RAM (about 100 ns), SSD (about 0.1 ms), and hard disk (about 10 ms). An arrow on the right indicates that the top is fast and the bottom is slow, and the text notes that lower levels have larger capacity and a lower price per unit of capacity.

explain: A **cache** is a small, fast memory placed close to the CPU. Programs show **locality**: data used recently is likely to be used again soon (**temporal locality**), and data near what was just used is likely to be used soon (**spatial locality**). So if frequently used data is kept in the cache, most accesses end in the cache. Performance is measured by the **average memory access time**. $$AMAT = \text{적중 시간} + \text{실패율} \times \text{실패 비용}$$ 적중 1 ns, 실패율 5%, 실패 비용 100 ns이면 $1 + 0.05 \times 100 = 6$ ns다.

The memory hierarchy runs from registers to cache (in several levels) to main memory to SSD or disk, and the higher levels are faster, smaller, and more expensive. When a programmer traverses data **sequentially**, the cache works well thanks to spatial locality. In a language that stores two-dimensional arrays row by row, traversing by column can make the same operation several times slower. Limitation: when several cores each have their own cache, a **cache coherence** problem arises, in which copies of the same data must be kept consistent with one another.

cs-11.title: Virtual Memory and Paging
explain: When several programs run at the same time, each behaves as if it alone uses the entire computer memory. Programs larger than the actual physical memory can also run. This illusion is created by **virtual memory**, which the operating system and hardware provide together.

Each process uses its own **virtual address space**. These addresses must be translated into **physical addresses** in real memory. The unit of translation is the **page**. The virtual address space is divided into pages of a fixed size (for example, 4 KB), and physical memory is divided into **frames** of the same size. The **page table** records which physical frame each virtual page is mapped to. A virtual address is split into (page number, offset within the page). If the page size is $2^k$ bytes, the lower $k$ bits of the address are the offset.

The benefits of virtual memory are: ① **isolation**, so one process cannot access another process's memory; ② **the illusion of contiguity**, so physically scattered frames are used as if they were one continuous virtual space; and ③ **demand paging**, so only the pages currently needed are loaded into memory and the rest stay on disk. Accessing a page that is not in memory causes a **page fault**, and the operating system fetches the page from disk.

When memory is full, the **page replacement algorithm** decides which page to evict. FIFO evicts the page that arrived longest ago. **LRU** (least recently used) evicts the page that has gone unused for the longest time and performs well because it exploits temporal locality. The theoretical optimal (OPT) evicts the page that will be needed latest in the future; it requires knowing the future and so cannot be used in practice, but it serves as a benchmark for comparison. Since page table translation also requires a memory access, a small cache that stores recent translations, called the **TLB**, is provided.

Limitation: disk access is tens to hundreds of thousands of times slower than memory access, so if page faults become too frequent, the CPU hardly does any work and only moves pages back and forth. This condition is called **thrashing**. It occurs when the **working set** of the running processes (the pages they have recently used frequently) does not fit in memory. The remedies are to reduce the number of simultaneously running processes or to add memory.

examples.title: Splitting an address
body: Given: a page size of 4 KB $= 2^{12}$ bytes, and a virtual address of 20,500 (decimal).

Step 2: If the page table maps virtual page 5 to physical frame 9, the physical address $= 9 \times 4096 + 20 = 36{,}884$.

cs-12.title: Process Scheduling and Deadlock
explain: A CPU core can do only one thing at a time, yet the computer appears to run dozens of programs simultaneously. This is because the operating system's **scheduler** switches among processes in very short time slices. The order of execution determines responsiveness and throughput. And when several processes share resources, a **deadlock** can occur, in which they wait forever for each other.

explain.alt: Two Gantt charts. All three processes arrive at time 0. In (a), P1 runs from 0 to 8, P2 from 8 to 12, and P3 from 12 to 14, in that order. In (b), P3 runs from 0 to 2, P2 from 2 to 6, and P1 from 6 to 14, in that order.

explain: Representative scheduling algorithms: **FCFS** (first come, first served) is simple, but it has a **convoy effect** in which short jobs queued behind a long job wait a long time. **SJF** (shortest job first) is proven to minimize the average waiting time, but execution times must be known in advance, and long jobs may suffer **starvation** as they keep being pushed back. **Round robin** gives each process a fixed time quantum and runs them in turn, which gives good responsiveness. If the quantum is too small, the switching cost grows; if it is too large, the behavior becomes similar to FCFS.

Evaluation metrics include **waiting time** (time spent waiting in the ready state), **turnaround time** (from arrival to completion), and **response time** (until first execution). In figure (a), with FCFS order, the waiting times are P1 0, P2 8, and P3 12, averaging about 6.67. In figure (b), with SJF order, they are P3 0, P2 2, and P1 6, averaging about 2.67. With the same jobs, changing only the order greatly reduced the average waiting time.

**Deadlock** is a state in which two or more processes wait for resources held by each other and stop forever. It occurs only when **all** four conditions hold (the Coffman conditions). ① **Mutual exclusion**: a resource can be used by only one process at a time. ② **Hold and wait**: a process holds a resource while waiting for another. ③ **No preemption**: a resource cannot be forcibly taken away from another process. ④ **Circular wait**: the waiting forms a cycle. Therefore, prevention means breaking one of the four conditions. For example, if every resource is numbered and processes are required to **always request lower-numbered resources first**, a circular wait cannot arise.

Limitations: real operating systems use complex schedulers, such as a multilevel feedback queue that mixes several criteria, and they estimate execution time from past behavior. Because prevention lowers resource utilization, some systems allow deadlocks to occur and then **detect and recover** from them, or treat them as rare and ignore them. The right choice depends on the purpose of the system (real-time control or a general-purpose PC).

Step 2: The completion times are P1 at 8 and P2 at 7. The waiting times are P1 $8 - 5 = 3$ and P2 $7 - 3 = 4$, for an average of 3.5. Both processes receive their first response quickly.

cs-13.title: Relational Model and SQL
explain: Data that many people must handle accurately at the same time, such as bank accounts, course registrations, and order histories, is stored in a **database management system** (DBMS). The most widely used kind is the relational database, which handles data as **tables (relations)**. This lesson covers the core concepts of the relational model and the essentials of **SQL**, the language used to work with it.

Terms of the relational model: **relation** (table), **tuple** (row, representing one entity), and **attribute** (column). The attribute, or set of attributes, that uniquely distinguishes each row is the **primary key** (for example, the student ID in a student table). An attribute that refers to the primary key of another table is a **foreign key** (for example, the student ID in an enrollment table refers to the student table). Foreign keys prevent contradictions such as an enrollment record for a non-existent student (**referential integrity**).

**Relational algebra** is the mathematical foundation of operations on tables. It includes **selection** (choosing rows that satisfy a condition), **projection** (keeping only the desired columns), **join** (linking two tables through a common attribute), union, and difference. SQL writes these as statements. `SELECT name FROM student WHERE grade = 2` means 'from the student table (FROM), select the rows where grade is 2 (WHERE), and project the name column (SELECT).'

The join is the power of relational databases. Joining Student (student ID, name) and Enrollment (student ID, course) by student ID gives 'who takes which course.' Grouping with **GROUP BY** and computing aggregates such as COUNT and AVG gives 'number of students per course.' SQL is a language that declares **what** you want, while **how** to fetch it (in what order to join and which index to use) is decided by the DBMS's query optimizer.

Limits and cautions: joins are expensive for large data. Joining on a non-key column, or joining without any condition, can make the number of rows explode multiplicatively (100,000 rows × 100,000 rows = 10 billion rows). Also, if user input is concatenated directly into an SQL statement, the system is exposed to **SQL injection** attacks, in which an attacker manipulates the statement. Input must be passed separately as parameters.

cs-14.title: Functional Dependencies and Normalization
explain: Putting all information into one large table may seem convenient. However, if a student's address is stored repeatedly for each course the student takes, every row must be changed when the address changes, and if even one row is missed, the data becomes contradictory. The systematic design method that eliminates such problems is **normalization**.

The three **anomalies** of an unnormalized design are: ① **update anomaly**: only some of the duplicated information is changed, creating a contradiction; ② **insertion anomaly**: a student who has not yet enrolled in any course (and therefore has no enrollment information) cannot be registered; ③ **deletion anomaly**: deleting a student's last enrollment record also deletes the student's information.

The foundation of normalization is **functional dependency**. When the value of attribute X uniquely determines the value of attribute Y, we write X → Y. Student ID → name, student ID → department, department → department head. **First normal form** (1NF): every attribute value is atomic and cannot be divided further (no multiple values in one cell). **Second normal form** (2NF): the table is in 1NF, and there is no attribute that depends on only **part** of the primary key (partial dependency). **Third normal form** (3NF): the table is in 2NF, and there is no attribute that depends on the key through a non-key attribute (transitive dependency; student ID → department → department head). **BCNF**: every determinant (the X in X → Y) is a candidate key.

Normalization is done by **decomposing** tables. In a table with (student ID, course, name, department, department head, grade) whose primary key is (student ID, course), name and department depend only on student ID (partial dependency), and the department head depends on it through the department (transitive dependency). Splitting this into Student (student ID, name, department), Department (department, department head), and Enrollment (student ID, course, grade) stores each fact in only one place. The decomposition must allow the original information to be restored **without loss** by joining the tables.

Limits and trade-offs: as normalization progresses, the number of tables increases, and queries can become slower because more joins are needed. In analytic systems where reads overwhelmingly dominate, **denormalization**, which intentionally allows duplication, is sometimes used. In that case, the application takes on the responsibility of keeping the duplicated data consistent. It is a choice between integrity and performance.

Step 2 (3NF): In the Student table, student ID → department → department head is a transitive dependency, so separate it into Department (department, department head). Now, when the department head changes, only one row in the Department table needs to be updated.

cs-15.title: Transactions, ACID, and Indexes
explain: The server went down in the middle of transferring 100,000 won from account A to account B. What if money left A but never arrived in B? Or what if two people book the same seat at the same time? A database must keep data accurate even in such situations. The promise that makes this possible is the **transaction** and its **ACID** properties. And what allows a desired row to be found quickly among hundreds of millions of rows is the **index**.

A **transaction** is a set of operations grouped into one logical unit of work (withdrawal and deposit). **ACID**: ① **Atomicity**: either all operations are executed or none are. If a failure occurs midway, the parts already done are reversed (rollback). ② **Consistency**: integrity constraints (such as a balance of at least 0 and a preserved total amount) hold before and after a transaction. ③ **Isolation**: concurrently running transactions do not see each other's intermediate states, so the results look as if they had been executed one after another. ④ **Durability**: once a transaction is complete (committed), its results survive even if a failure occurs (recorded in a log).

A representative way to preserve isolation is **locking**. Data is locked before it is read or written, and other transactions wait until the lock is released. Perfect isolation greatly reduces concurrency, so the DBMS provides several **isolation levels**. Lower levels are faster but allow reading uncommitted values (dirty reads) and results of the same query changing midway. Using locks can cause a **deadlock**, as covered in Stage 3, so the DBMS detects deadlocks and cancels one of the transactions.

An **index** is a separate structure, like the index at the back of a book, that quickly finds row positions from the values of a specific column. The standard structure is the **B+ tree**, a wide, shallow balanced tree whose nodes hold hundreds of keys. This is because disk reads happen in blocks, so fetching many keys in one read is advantageous. If each node has $b$ children, the height is about $\log_b n$. With $b = 100$ and $n = 10^8$, the height is 4, so finding one row among 100 million takes 4 block reads. The leaf nodes are linked together, so range searches are also fast.

Limitations: indexes are not free. Every insertion or modification of data also requires the indexes to be updated, which slows down writes and takes storage space. Indexing a column with few distinct values, such as gender, provides little benefit. Indexes should be chosen for columns used in frequently queried conditions and in joins.

cs-16.title: Network Layer Models and TCP Congestion Control
explain: In Stage 1, we saw an outline of how a web page arrives. This time we look at the principles by which the Internet connects billions of devices reliably, dividing them into **layers**. We also cover **TCP congestion control**, which keeps the Internet from clogging and ensures it is shared fairly.

Internet protocols are divided into layers. The **application layer** (HTTP, DNS) determines what is exchanged; the **transport layer** (TCP, UDP) handles delivery between processes; the **network layer** (IP) finds a path from the source computer to the destination computer; and the **link layer** (Ethernet, Wi-Fi) delivers data to the directly adjacent device. Each layer uses the service of the layer below and provides a service to the layer above. As data goes down the layers, a header is added at each layer (encapsulation), and the receiving side removes them one by one.

**TCP** provides reliable transmission. It uses sequence numbers and acknowledgments (ACKs) to resend lost data and to put data back in order. **UDP** sends quickly without such guarantees (suitable for real-time voice and video, where delay is worse than occasional loss). TCP exchanges three messages when starting a connection (the three-way handshake).

The window doubles every RTT, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, until it reaches the threshold of 16 shown as a dashed line, and then grows by 1 each RTT, 17, 18, 19, 20. At the 8th RTT, after 'loss detected,' it drops to 10 and then grows by 1 each RTT, 11, 12, 13, 14.

explain: **Congestion control**: if every sender transmits at maximum speed, the buffers of routers overflow and packets are discarded, and retransmissions make the congestion even worse. TCP adjusts the **congestion window** (the amount that can be sent without acknowledgment). **Slow start**: it begins at 1 and doubles the window every round trip (RTT). When it reaches the **threshold**, it switches to **congestion avoidance** and increases the window by only 1 per RTT. When a loss is detected, the window is reduced (halved, as in the figure). This method of "increase additively, decrease multiplicatively" (AIMD) makes multiple connections share bandwidth roughly fairly.

The throughput of TCP is roughly $\frac{\text{윈도 크기}}{\text{RTT}}$. With a window of 64 KB and an RTT of 100 ms, it is about 640 KB/s. A long-distance connection with a long RTT has lower throughput with the same window. Limitation: on wireless networks, packets are lost due to radio propagation problems rather than congestion, but traditional TCP mistakes this for congestion and unnecessarily slows down. For this reason, improved congestion control algorithms, such as ones that use changes in delay, continue to be studied.

cs-17.title: IP Addresses and Routing
explain: To send a letter, you need an address, and the post office looks at the address to decide which direction to send it. On the Internet, **IP addresses** and **routers** play this role. This lesson covers how addresses are structured and how packets find their way among countless possible paths.

An IPv4 address is 32 bits long and is usually written as four decimal numbers, each representing 8 bits (192.168.10.5). An address is divided into a **network part** and a **host part**, and the boundary is indicated by a **subnet mask** or a prefix length (/24). 192.168.10.0/24 means that the first 24 bits are the network and the last 8 bits are the host. This network has $2^8 = 256$ addresses. After excluding the network address and the broadcast address, 254 can be assigned to devices.

32 bits can produce only about 4.3 billion addresses, which has become insufficient. There are two responses. **NAT**: inside a home or company, private addresses are used, and when traffic leaves the network, the home router replaces them with a single public address. **IPv6**: 128-bit addresses, so there is virtually no concern about running out.

**Routing**: each router has a **routing table** and, based on the destination address, decides which neighbor (the next hop) to send the packet to. If several entries match, the entry with the **longest prefix** match is chosen, meaning the more specific route takes priority. Routing tables are built automatically as routers exchange information with each other. Within a single organization, a method such as OSPF is used, in which every router is told the state of all links and computes shortest paths with the **Dijkstra algorithm** (covered in Stage 2). Between organizations, a path-vector method that reflects policies (BGP) is used.

Limitations: routing is affected not only by the 'shortest' path but also by cost, contracts, and policies. If incorrect path information spreads, communication over a wide area can be sent to the wrong place or cut off, so verifying path information is an important issue for Internet security. This lesson is an introduction to principles; it does not cover how to configure networks or how to check security.

cs-18.title: Foundations of Cryptography: Symmetric Keys, Public Keys, and Hashes
explain: When passwords and payment information are sent over the Internet, the data passes through many other people's devices. **Cryptography** is the set of mathematical tools that prevent anyone from peeking at or altering the data. This lesson covers the principles and roles of three basic tools. Attacks on actual systems and ways to bypass them are not covered.

The three goals of security are **confidentiality** (only authorized people can see the content), **integrity** (confirming that the content has not been changed), and **authentication** (confirming that the other party really is who they claim to be). Each of the three tools serves a different goal.

**Symmetric-key cryptography** uses the **same key** for encryption and decryption (AES is an example). It is fast and efficient, so it is used to encrypt large amounts of data. Its problem is **key distribution**: how can a secret key be shared safely with a party you are meeting for the first time? Also, for $n$ people to communicate with a different key for each pair, $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ keys are needed, which makes management difficult as the number of people grows.

**Public-key cryptography** uses a pair consisting of a **public key** and a **private key**. Data encrypted with the public key can be decrypted only with its partner, the private key. Since the public key can be disclosed to anyone, the key distribution problem disappears. The principle relies on mathematical problems that are easy in one direction and very hard in the reverse. RSA uses the fact that multiplying two large primes is easy but factoring the product back into primes is very hard, together with modular arithmetic (Fermat's and Euler's theorems). Public-key cryptography is slow, so in practice it is used to **securely exchange a symmetric key**, and the data itself is then encrypted with that symmetric key. This is how HTTPS on the web works.

A **hash function** converts data of arbitrary length into a digest of fixed length. A good cryptographic hash satisfies four properties: ① the same input always gives the same output; ② it is hard to recover the input from the output; ③ it is hard to find a different input with the same output (a collision); and ④ even a tiny change to the input changes the output completely. Hashes are used to verify file integrity and to store passwords (a hash is stored together with a salt value instead of the original password). Signing a document's hash with a private key creates a **digital signature**, which guarantees both authentication and integrity. Limitations: if key management breaks down or the implementation is flawed, even strong mathematics is of no use. Also, quantum computers may threaten some of today's public-key cryptography, so new cryptographic methods are being researched and standardized.

cs-19.title: Capstone Problem Solving: Diagnosing a Bottleneck in a Virtual Service
explain: The first lesson of the capstone diagnoses one virtual service using knowledge from Stages 2 to 5. The situation: the online lecture site "Baeumteo" has lecture list pages that take several seconds each time its users increase tenfold, and occasionally a course registration is processed twice.

**Step 1 (measure)**: measure before guessing. Dividing the time of a single request into segments showed 0.1 seconds for the network, 0.2 seconds for application computation, and 2.5 seconds for the database query. The bottleneck is the database. As with the bottleneck principle from Stage 2, unless the slowest segment is fixed, speeding up the other segments will not help much.

**Step 2 (database)**: analyzing the queries showed that finding lectures with 'field = mathematics' in the lecture table (500,000 rows) was scanning the entire table without an index. Adding an index on the field column changes the $O(n)$ full scan into a B+ tree search. Also, the number of enrollees for each lecture was being calculated with COUNT every time. Since this value is read frequently, denormalization that stores it in a separate column should be considered, but it must be updated within the same transaction as the enrollment to keep it consistent.

**Step 3 (cache)**: the lecture list is read often and changes rarely. Storing the results in an in-memory cache means most requests never reach the database. If the hit rate is 90%, the cache response is 5 ms, and the database response is 300 ms, the average response is $= 0.9 \times 5 + 0.1 \times 300 = 34.5$ ms. This is the same calculation as the AMAT in Stage 3. However, when a lecture changes, the cache must be invalidated so that outdated lists are not shown.

**Step 4 (duplicate registration error)**: when the same user presses the button twice quickly, both requests checked 'not yet registered' at the same time, and both recorded a registration. This is a **race condition** caused by insufficient isolation. Countermeasures: place a uniqueness constraint on the (student, lecture) pair so that the database rejects duplicates, and group the check and the recording into a single transaction. **Critique**: introducing a cache creates new consistency problems, and indexes slow down writes. Each improvement must be verified by measurement.

Step 2: The load on the database falls to 5% of requests, one-twentieth of the original. If the hit rate is set lower, at 90%, the average is 23.6 ms and the load is 10%.

However, since the field has only a few distinct values, if the 'mathematics' lectures make up half of all lectures, the effect of the index is small (this is called selectivity).

cs-20.title: Undergraduate Capstone: Service System Design Document
explain: The final task is to **choose one hypothetical service, write a system design document for it, analyze its expected bottlenecks and risks, and critique the trade-offs in the design**. This is not a real service or a security audit, and it is not a coding assignment. It develops the ability to explain the reasoning behind a design in words.

Structure of the design document: ① **Requirements**: functional (what it does) and non-functional (number of concurrent users, response time target, availability). ② **Data design**: main entities and tables, keys and foreign keys, and the level of normalization and the reason for it. ③ **Core operations and algorithms**: the most frequent operations and their complexity, and the required indexes and data structures. ④ **Performance design**: expected bottlenecks, the cache strategy and invalidation, and estimates (number of requests × processing time). ⑤ **Correctness**: where transactions are needed, concurrency problems, and countermeasures. ⑥ **Network and security**: communication encryption, password storage, and input validation. ⑦ **Trade-offs and critique**: what was gained and what was given up.

Features of a good design document: it estimates with numbers (for example, "1,000 requests per second × 2 queries = 2,000 queries per second"). It records the **reason** and the **alternatives** for every choice. It does not hide trade-offs, such as consistency versus speed, or simplicity versus scalability. Parts deferred with 'we will think about it later' are also recorded in the list of risks.
The task is not graded. The submitted text is saved only on this device and can be viewed again under 'My Notes' in 'My Progress'.

Correctness: double booking of the same seat is prevented by combining the uniqueness constraint with a transaction.
Performance: the list of empty seats is cached for a short time (a few seconds), while final booking confirmation is always checked against the database.
Critique: a user may see a seat as empty in the cached list and then fail to book it. In that case, the latest list is shown again immediately upon failure.
